text: The cosmos is another word for the whole universe: every star, planet, galaxy and empty stretch of space there is. It comes from a Greek word meaning order, because the ancient Greeks saw the sky as an orderly system rather than a mess. To map the cosmos means to chart what is out there and where it sits.

NASA is the space agency of the United States government, set up in 1958. The letters stand for National Aeronautics and Space Administration. It builds and flies spacecraft, runs telescopes, and pays for a large share of the world's space science.

This is NASA's newest big space telescope, launched on August 30th and usually just called Roman. It is named after Nancy Grace Roman, the first chief astronomer at NASA, who pushed for putting telescopes above the atmosphere. Its job is to photograph huge patches of sky in one shot rather than tiny patches in great detail.

Universal Time is the single world clock scientists use so that everyone means the same instant, no matter which time zone they are in. It runs on the time at Greenwich, in London. Saying the rocket left at 11.26 Universal Time avoids the confusion of one person saying morning and another saying evening.

The Kennedy Space Centre is NASA's launch site on the coast of Florida, named after President John F. Kennedy. Rockets fly east from there out over the Atlantic, so anything that goes wrong falls into empty ocean. The Economist is a British magazine, which is why it spells centre with the r before the e.

SpaceX is a private American rocket company founded by Elon Musk in 2002. NASA no longer builds most of its own rockets; it buys rides from companies like this one. So the telescope belongs to NASA, but the rocket underneath it did not.

Falcon Heavy is SpaceX's biggest working rocket, made of three Falcon 9 boosters strapped side by side. It is used for the heaviest loads and the ones that must be flung the furthest from Earth. Roman needed it because its parking spot is more than a million kilometres away.

An eye in the sky is anything high above that watches what is below, such as a security camera, a police helicopter or a satellite. Here the phrase is flipped around: this eye sits in the sky but looks outward, away from Earth. It is a quick way of saying the telescope is NASA's newest way of seeing.

An astronomer is a scientist who studies objects beyond Earth, such as stars, planets and galaxies. Almost all of their evidence arrives as light, so most of the job is collecting light carefully and working out what it means. Do not mix them up with astronauts, who fly, or astrologers, who make horoscopes.

Here the m is short for million, not metres, so this means 1.6 million kilometres. British writing shortens numbers this way all the time: 3m people, 5bn dollars. That distance is about four times as far as the Moon.

An orbit is the curved path one object takes as it circles another under the pull of gravity, like the Moon around Earth. Something in orbit is falling forwards so fast that it keeps missing what it is falling towards. The telescope will orbit far from Earth, and the planets it hunts orbit their own stars.

Unprecedented means nothing like it has happened before, so there is no earlier example to compare it with. A precedent is an earlier case that sets the pattern, and the un at the front takes that away. Calling Roman's view of the universe unprecedented claims that no telescope before it has shown astronomers this much sky in this much detail.

The Wide Field Instrument, or WFI, is Roman's main camera. Wide field means it takes in a large piece of sky at once instead of zooming in on a small one. That is the whole point of the mission: less detail per star, far more stars per picture.

A pixel is one tiny dot of a digital picture, and a megapixel is a million of them. A phone camera is usually around 12 to 50 megapixels, so a 300-megapixel camera records a picture roughly six to twenty-five times bigger. More pixels means you can cover more sky without the image turning into a blur.

Visible light is the narrow band of light human eyes can actually detect, running from red at one end to violet at the other. It is only a sliver of all the light that exists. Roman sees this band and also infrared, which sits just past red where your eyes stop working.

Infrared is light with waves slightly longer than red light, which is why the name means below red. Your eyes cannot see it, but your skin feels the strongest kind as heat, and a TV remote sends its signal with it. Space telescopes care about it because the light from very distant galaxies arrives stretched into this range.

A galaxy is an enormous group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity, usually containing billions of stars. Ours is the Milky Way, and the Sun is one star inside it. Distant galaxies are the furthest things telescopes can photograph, so their light is also the oldest.

Light travels as waves, and a wavelength is the distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next. Short wavelengths look blue to us and long ones look red, with infrared longer still. Stretching light to a longer wavelength shifts it towards the red and infrared end.

Astronomers found in the 1920s that distant galaxies are all getting further from us: space itself is stretching, like the surface of a balloon being blown up. Light crossing that stretching space gets stretched too, so its waves arrive longer than they started. That is why the light of very distant galaxies shows up as infrared rather than visible light.

A field of view is how much of a scene an eye, a camera or a telescope can take in at one moment. Look through a drinking straw and your field of view shrinks to a dot; drop the straw and it opens up again. Roman's field of view is over 100 times larger than Hubble's, so one Roman photograph replaces a hundred Hubble ones.

A predecessor is whoever or whatever came before, such as the person who held a job before you or the older model a new one replaces. The word hides precede, meaning to come before. Hubble is Roman's predecessor because Hubble did this job first.

Hubble is the famous NASA space telescope launched in 1990 and still working, named after the astronomer Edwin Hubble. It takes extremely sharp pictures of small patches of sky. Roman trades some of that sharpness for a far wider view.

Paradoxically flags something that sounds like it contradicts itself but is still true. Here the odd-sounding truth is that two of the camera's main targets will never show up in its photographs. The word warns you that the next sentence will not work the way you expect.

Dark matter is material that gives off no light at all, so no telescope can photograph it. Astronomers are sure it exists because galaxies spin far too fast to hold together on the gravity of their visible stars alone; something heavy and unseen must be pulling. Nobody yet knows what it is actually made of.

Dark energy is the name for whatever is making the universe expand faster and faster instead of slowing down. Astronomers measured the speeding up in 1998 and had no explanation for it, so they gave the unknown cause a name. Like dark matter it is invisible, and dark here means unknown as much as unlit.

A phenomenon is any event or thing that can be observed, and phenomena is its plural, so you say one phenomenon but two phenomena. Scientists use it for something they can measure without yet being able to explain. Dark matter and dark energy are called phenomena precisely because their effects show up but their nature does not.

Spacetime is the idea, from Albert Einstein, that the three directions of space and the flow of time are one connected thing rather than two separate ones. Heavy objects bend it, and that bending is what we experience as gravity. Astronomers spot dark matter by measuring how starlight gets bent as it passes through the bent spacetime around it.

Souped-up describes something that has been modified to perform better than the standard version, most often a car engine. It is casual, everyday English rather than a technical term. Roman's souped-up optics are simply lenses and mirrors far better than the usual ones.

Optics are the parts of an instrument that gather and steer light: the mirrors, lenses and filters. Optics is also the name of the branch of physics that studies how light behaves. In a telescope the optics decide how much light you catch and how sharp the result is.

An oddity is something strange or out of the ordinary, from the word odd. Calling dark matter and dark energy cosmic oddities is a mild, slightly amused way of saying they do not fit anything else we know. It is not an insult, just an admission that they are peculiar.

An exoplanet is a planet that orbits a star other than our Sun. The exo part comes from a Greek word for outside, so an exoplanet is a planet outside our solar system. The first one was confirmed in 1992, and about 6,000 are known today.

Far-flung means spread out over a great distance, or simply very far away. It comes from flinging something a long way. Far-flung stars are the ones scattered across the sky well beyond our own neighbourhood.

Alien here just means belonging somewhere else, not creatures with spaceships. An alien world is a planet outside our solar system, whether or not anything lives on it. The everyday meaning of alien as a foreigner or an outsider comes from the same root.

A blip is a small, brief change in a signal, like the dot that flashes on a radar screen. In this article the blips are tiny dips in how bright a star looks, lasting hours and then vanishing. They matter because that dip is the shadow of a planet crossing in front of the star.

To emit something is to send it out, so light emitted by a star is light the star produces and releases. Emit is used for light, sound, heat, smells and gases. It is the opposite of absorb, which means to take in.

A coronagraph is a device inside a telescope that blocks the light of a star so that fainter things beside it become visible. It works like holding your thumb up to hide the Sun so you can see what is next to it. It was invented in the 1930s to study the Sun's outer glow, the corona, which is where the name comes from.

Dmitry Savransky is an engineering professor at Cornell University who works on Roman's coronagraph. He is the person quoted in this article explaining which stars the instrument will aim at. British publications write Dr rather than Dr. with a full stop.

Cornell University is a large research university in Ithaca, New York, founded in 1865. Universities like it design and build instruments for NASA missions under contract. So the coronagraph is a NASA instrument built with help from university scientists.

A light-year is a distance, not an amount of time: it is how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometres. Astronomers use it because writing star distances in kilometres would take fourteen digits. Within 100 light-years counts as nearby in astronomy, even though the nearest star of all is 4.2 light-years off.

A host star is the star a particular planet orbits; the Sun is Earth's host star. The word host is used the way it is for a party, meaning the one everything else gathers around. Planets are hard to photograph because their host star sits right beside them and is millions of times brighter.

Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system, a ball of gas about eleven times wider than Earth. Size is why it comes up here: a big planet catches and reflects far more starlight than a small rocky one. Roman's coronagraph should manage pictures of Jupiter-sized worlds, while Earth-sized ones stay out of reach.

Arduous means hard, tiring and long, the kind of difficulty that drags on rather than a single tough moment. It usually describes a journey, a climb or a stretch of work. The telescope's arduous journey to the launch pad was the years of building it and the fight over paying for it, not the flight itself.

A launch pad is the reinforced concrete platform a rocket stands on and lifts off from. Getting to the launch pad is a common way of saying a project finally made it to the starting line. In this sentence the real journey being described is the twenty years of work before liftoff.

In American politics, an administration means a president and the officials who run the government under them, so the Trump administration means Donald Trump's government. It has nothing to do with office paperwork. Each administration proposes how much money government agencies like NASA should get.

To scrap something is to cancel it and throw it away before or instead of finishing it, the way an old car is scrapped for metal. It is much stronger than delaying or shrinking a project. The proposal was to cancel the Roman telescope entirely, after most of it had already been built.

Funding is money supplied to pay for something over time, usually by a government, a company or a donor. A fund is a pot of money set aside for a purpose, and funding is the act of filling it. Science funding is what pays the salaries, parts and testing behind a mission like this one.

Saying someone might be forgiven for feeling a certain way is a polite English way of saying that feeling would be completely fair. It hands out permission for a reaction the writer thinks is justified. Here it means the scientists had every right to feel confused when the president who tried to cancel their telescope turned up to celebrate it.

t: put that money where his mouth is
forms: put that money where his mouth is
text: To put your money where your mouth is means to actually spend or risk something to back up what you have been saying, instead of just talking. The usual form is put your money where your mouth is, and the article bends it to fit. The closing line is a nudge: having taken credit for the launch, he should keep paying for the science.
